comments.author: @philstewart2245
comments.text: I was wondering if the Sir John Johnson mentioned in the video is the same Lt col John Johnson whose grave I found in Port Maitland near Dunville.   The grave stone mentions that Lt Col Johnson was formerly of the Bombay Engineers, the private army of the British East India Company, and was a member of the Order of the Bath, one of Queen Victoria's favourite awards.  I assumed that he was in that area working on the Welland canal.  He passed away around 1870, and must have lived a very interesting life.  His wife who lived into the 1880's is interred next to him. Mrs Johnson had a very unique first name that suggested to me she may have been Indian.

replies.author: @philstewart2245
replies.text: @HiddenCanada The grave yard at the old Anglican church on the lake is a treasure trove of history that would deserve a future video.  There is a mass grave containing 50 bodies, members and dependants of the Irish Regiment.  The regiment was changing postings from Wolsley Barracks, London, Canada West to Fort Henry, Kinston, in 1850.  The steam ship "commerce" foundered in a storm and there was loss of life.There is a marker for the 50 un identified bodies that washed ashore and two identified graves of a pair of officers of the Irish Regiment.  The irony of it all was that the Commerce does not appear on a list of lake Erie ship wrecks because it was salvaged, re named Caribou, and served on the lakes for many more years before being scrapped.  Thank you for your response correcting a few of my mis recollections of the grave stones, it has been quite a while since I visited the graves.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: What an interesting find! I looked into it, and they're actually two different John Johnsons. Sir John Johnson, the Loyalist, died in 1830 and was buried in Quebec. The officer you found in Port Maitland was Lieutenant-Colonel John Johnson of the Bombay Engineers, who died in 1846. His wife was named Dederika, and she died in 1850. I even found a local history documenting his family's arrival in the area! Thanks for sharing this. You've sent me down another fascinating history rabbit hole!

comments.author: @jean-pierredecouvreur9500
comments.text:
Very dramatic and partly false reporting..."in all my research", you say? Your research should have revealed that the ban on human activity (trespassing) is not for the whole of the bay, and not even for the whole of the sandy spit on the Lake Ontario side of the bay. 

Your research should have revealed that the people who go to the beach do so in an area of Weller's Bay where it is perfectly legal to go. This is the kilometer or so of the spit from the chanel at Barcovan, towards the South. The lake Ontario side has a beautiful sandy beach, the shallow sandy bottom extending far out into the lake (can stand on the bottom as far out as 150m) and providing quite warm waters due to the shallow sandy bottom absorbing the sun's rays and relatively less lake wave action. The lakeside's beach is unbroken for the whole length (about one kilometer) while on the bay side, there are only two small areas where one can use the shore. While smaller "beaches" mean less people can use the area, it is also much more sheltered and the waters very shallow and warm. Both sides of the spit can only be reached by boat/canoe/kayak, although some people occasionally walk across the chanel from Barcovan, holding their beach towels over their heads, when the lake waters are low enough.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: You're right, Jean-Pierre, and I appreciate you taking the time to explain this. I should have made it clearer that the restrictions don't apply to the entire bay or the whole sand spit. The northern section near Barcovan is outside the National Wildlife Area and is used recreationally. I can see how the video might have given the wrong impression about people visiting that stretch of beach. That's a fair criticism, and I'll be more careful with that distinction in future videos. Thanks for pointing it out!

comments.author: @genghiscalm4879
comments.text:
Stayed at one of the campgrounds. Mid 80s. I was a teen. A bunch of us went out to that beach one afternoon. Was walking on the shallow bay side of the spit when I very nearly fell over an old milk can buried in the sand. First instinct was to curse and kick it. Second instinct was to back very slowly away from it. Yep. Not a milk can. A damned bomb half showing in the silty water.
We reported it. My time was up, but one of the other guys showed DND where it was. I'm told a sniper was brought in to detonate it. I was very likely one step away from being fish food.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Wow, that was a frighteningly close call! I'm glad your second instinct was to back away instead of kicking it. It's one thing reading about unexploded bombs in government records, but hearing from someone who actually encountered one back in the 80s really puts those warnings into perspective. Do you remember roughly where along the spit you found it? Thanks for sharing your experience, and I'm glad you're here to tell the story!

comments.author: @chrismurray9489
comments.text: My aunt had a place in Barcovan Bay. We used to go to beaches on different islands in the early 80s. Everyone knew there was ordinance around. Old wire fences with DND signs were everywhere. We never saw anything.  Great beaches.

replies.author: @chrismurray9489
replies.text:
​@HiddenCanada I haven't been out there in years.  We just called them "The Islands". They're probably all one long one now. The sand moves alot.  

When my uncle wasn't able to take us out on the boat, we'd swim across a narrow channel right off of Barcovan Beach Road. It was maybe 30 feet across, but deep.

The wire fence I mentioned was giving it a lot of credit. Most of it I saw was rusted, broken and laying in the sand. We had to watch our step when going from the sand into the vegetation.   It sounds funny saying we watched our step to avoid rusty fencing on an island with ordinance on it, but we were kids. 😂

The DND signs were plain, white with red letters. They had a phone number on it to report found ordinance.  We thought that was kind of funny, because calling it meant you'd be in trouble with the OPP.

I know we have some photos from the beach, but I haven't seen them in a long time. It was a popular spot in the 80s.
